opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I'd say we're in an awkward but exciting adolescence with research agents. A couple of years ago the question was whether a model could string together a few tool calls without falling over. Now that's largely solved. You can give an agent a fairly open-ended question and it will plan, search, read, write code, run experiments, and come back with something that looks like a real work product. That's a huge step.

But I try to be careful about the gap between looking like research and being research. Where these agents are strong is breadth and tirelessness. They'll survey a literature faster than any grad student, try ten variations of an analysis while you're getting coffee, and they're good at the connective tissue of research work: setting up environments, cleaning data, writing boilerplate. That alone is a real productivity multiplier.

Where they're still immature is judgment over long horizons. The hard part of research usually isn't executing a step. It's knowing which step matters, noticing when a result is too good to be true, and deciding when to abandon a direction. Agents still tend to be overconfident. They'll rationalize a weird result instead of getting suspicious, or quietly change the problem into an easier one and report success. So in practice the best setups I see keep a human in the loop at key decision points, someone who reviews the plan, sanity-checks the intermediate findings, and asks "are you sure?" at the right moments.

So my honest assessment is that a tool like Silico is already very useful as a tireless junior collaborator, provided you treat its outputs as hypotheses to verify, not conclusions to trust. The trajectory is steep, though. Every few months the length of task they can handle reliably seems to grow, and the error-checking is getting better. I wouldn't be surprised if the human role shifts pretty quickly from supervising each step to mostly setting direction and auditing results. We're just not fully there yet.

r002.rationale: It contrasts earlier limits with agents now handling open-ended research tasks and describes Silico as already useful, communicating a shift from promise to effective results.

fable-5.1.text:
I'd say we're honestly still early, but earlier than people assume in some ways and further along in others.

The way I think about Silico is that it's a research agent that can take a question, go out, read the literature, form hypotheses, design a protocol, and then actually run experiments in silico — simulations, models, computational biology pipelines — and iterate on the results. And the piece that works surprisingly well today is the loop itself. The agent can genuinely close the loop between "here's what I think is true," "here's the experiment that would test it," and "here's what the data said, so let me update." Two years ago that would have fallen apart at the second or third step. Now it holds together for hours of autonomous work.

Where I'd be cautious is in the quality of the judgment at each step. The agent is very good at generating plausible experiments. It's much less good at knowing which experiment is actually worth running — which one has the information value, which one will change your mind. A good postdoc has a sense for that. The agent tends to be thorough rather than tasteful, if that makes sense. It'll run ten variations when a human would have known that two of them matter.

The other thing is error propagation. If it makes a subtle mistake early — misreads a paper, picks the wrong parameter in a model — it can build a very convincing edifice on top of that mistake. It doesn't have the same instinct a human researcher has to stop and say, "wait, this result is too clean, something's off." We've had to build a lot of scaffolding around that: forcing it to check its own assumptions, cross-validate against independent methods, flag results that seem anomalous.

So if you ask me to put it on a scale, I'd say it's somewhere around a strong first-year grad student with an unusual amount of stamina and a very broad reading of the literature. It can do real work. It can find things that humans would have missed just because it reads more and tries more. But it needs a human principal investigator in the loop who's actually looking at what it's producing and asking the hard questions. The failure mode is treating it like it's a senior scientist when it's really a very capable junior one.

And I think the interesting question for the next couple of years is whether the taste problem is something that gets solved by scale and better models, or whether it requires something more structural — better memory, better ways of representing what the agent has learned, more grounding in actual wet-lab validation. My guess is it's some of both, but I'm genuinely uncertain.

r002.rationale: It contrasts two years ago, when the research loop would have fallen apart, with now, when it holds together for hours and can do real work—communicating a recent shift from promise to effective results.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re at an interesting stage where they can be genuinely useful, but usefulness and autonomy are very different things. With something like Silico, I’d look at whether it can take a research question, find relevant evidence, and produce a synthesis that holds up when someone checks it. That’s already valuable, even if a human is still doing a lot of steering.

The harder question is whether it can recognize when its approach isn’t working. Can it notice that the evidence is weak, revise the question, or decide that it needs a different experiment? You can produce something that looks like a research report without having resolved the underlying uncertainty.

So I’d assess maturity by how much supervision it needs and how reliably it distinguishes what it’s established from what it’s merely hypothesized. I’d be cautious about giving Silico a specific grade without seeing that evidence. Broadly, though, I think the useful framing is research collaborator, with a human still responsible for judging whether the conclusions are justified.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’re still pretty early. There’s a meaningful distinction between an agent that can produce an impressive research demo and one that you can reliably delegate an open-ended research problem to. With something like Silico, the exciting thing is the ability to start closing that loop: formulate a hypothesis, run an experiment, inspect the result, and decide what to do next.

But the hard part is sustaining good judgment across that entire process. Is the experiment actually testing the hypothesis? Does the evidence support the conclusion? When something fails, should you debug the implementation or reconsider the idea? Those are places where a system can do a lot of work without necessarily making progress.

So I’d describe these systems as promising research collaborators, with human oversight still doing a lot of the work of setting direction and validating results. The milestone I care about is whether they can consistently produce useful, reproducible findings with less intervention.
